title: DOM and events
summary: Select elements in the page tree, change their content and classes, and react to events as they bubble through the tree.

concepts.title: The DOM tree and selecting elements

misconceptions.description: Believes a selector that matches nothing returns undefined or an empty list instead of null.
Believes querySelectorAll returns a real array, so map, filter and the rest all work.
Believes querySelectorAll stops at the first match, or that a list holds a single element.
Reads a variable at the wrong moment of the run, such as the first pass or the final value.
Believes classList.add adds a class again when the element already has it.
Believes assigning textContent adds to the old text instead of replacing it.
Believes assigning textContent changes only the element's own text and keeps its child elements.
Believes classList.toggle always adds the class and never removes it.
Believes addEventListener runs the handler once when it is added, not only when the event happens.
Believes writing handler() and handler in addEventListener mean the same thing.
Believes a listener is removed after it runs once.
Believes handlers or events run in the order they appear in the file or on the page, not the order they were registered, triggered or travel.
Believes a click only calls the listeners on the clicked element, not on its ancestors.
Believes a listener on a parent works only for children that existed when it was added.

conceptCard.title: The page is a tree of elements
conceptCard.body: The DOM is a tree: every element can have children, which you reach through properties like children and firstElementChild. querySelector returns the first element that matches a CSS selector, or null. querySelectorAll returns all matches. The object below is a tiny model of such a tree.

conceptCard.title: Changing what the page shows
conceptCard.body: Assigning textContent replaces everything inside an element, child elements too. classList.add, remove and toggle change one class and leave the others. createElement makes a new element, and appendChild puts it into the page. A plain object models the element here.

conceptCard.title: A function the page calls later
conceptCard.body: addEventListener(type, handler) stores a function that the browser calls each time that event happens. Pass the function itself, never a call to it. The page keeps the stored handlers; an array plays that part below.

conceptCard.title: Events travel up the tree
conceptCard.body: An event starts at its target, then bubbles up through every ancestor, calling their listeners. One listener on a parent can handle all its children (delegation). The browser passes the handler an event e: e.target is the element that started it, e.currentTarget the one whose listener runs. target.matches(selector) tests it; target.closest(selector) finds it or its nearest matching ancestor.
conceptCard.expectedOutput:
reached button
reached li
reached ul

items.prompt: The page lists three trains. What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. Three elements match, index 1 is the second train, and no element has class bus, so null.
You thought a selector that matches nothing gives undefined, like a missing property. querySelector uses a value of its own to report that nothing matched.
You thought querySelectorAll stops at the first match, so the length would be 1. It collects every matching element, and the page lists several trains.

items.explanation: querySelectorAll returns every match, so the list holds 3 trains. Index 1 is the second one, Bergen. querySelector returns null, not undefined, when nothing matches.
hints: Count the elements with class train in the drawn tree.
Lists start at index 0. A selector that matches nothing gives a special empty value.
Check the first number against your count, then ask what a selector with no match returns.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

A NodeList looks like an array but is a different kind of object.
One printed word says a method exists, the other says it does not.

items.prompt: A heading is changed twice. What does this code print?

options.feedback: Right. The text is replaced, and the second add does nothing.
You thought calling classList.add twice writes the class twice. add looks at the classes the element already has, so repeating a name does not grow the list.
You thought assigning to textContent adds to the old text. An assignment to textContent replaces what was there; it does not append.

items.explanation: Assigning textContent replaces the old text, so the heading reads Soup 2. classList.add skips a class the element already has, so big appears once.
hints: Compare the heading text before and after line 3.
Assignment replaces the content. A class list never holds the same class twice.

options.text: It changes only the element's own text and keeps its children
options.feedback: You thought the child elements survive an assignment to textContent. They are part of what the element contains, and the assignment treats all of it as old content.

options.text: It adds the new text after the existing content
options.feedback: You thought the new text is added after the existing content. The assignment treats everything inside the element as old content, so nothing of it stays for the new text to follow.

items.explanation: Assigning to textContent replaces everything inside the element, child elements included. The two li elements are gone, so children.length drops to 0.
hints: Compare the two printed lengths.
textContent covers the whole content of an element, not only the text next to its children.

You thought addEventListener runs the handler when it is added. Registering only stores the function for later; show is called when a click arrives.
You thought a listener is removed after it runs once. A listener stays registered until it is removed, so each click calls it again.

items.explanation: The click starts on the button and bubbles up through its ancestors. The handler runs for the button, then the item, then the list, whatever order the listeners were added in.
